item.title: The Whistle: 61,000 probe pull requests, a stolen cookie into XCP-ng, and Nvidia's interim era
item.description: Stolen GitHub credentials sat at the front of this week’s news: a campaign that probed its way into 61,764 repositories in under two days and exfiltrated credentials from at least 1,835 of them. Behind it ran a takeover chain in Xen Orchestra that ended at XCP-ng root, and an AI-vendor breach whose third chapter reached into Notion’s customer set. On the product side, AWS shipped an emulator built end to end by agents, Google cut the nodepool ceremony out of TPU scheduling, Rust passed 1.100 with a type that took a decade, and Nvidia moved into an interim era without its founder. Security leads, then everything else.

item.title: The Whistle: Chrome's eighth zero-day, Qubole's trusted path, and an AI proof of Signal
item.description: Google patched Chrome’s eighth in-the-wild zero-day of the year, Wiz published an October attack that walked through the front door Qubole customers built for their own data platform, and a researcher’s 33 zero-days made an RMM vendor unplug its own hosted service. Anthropic put a security model behind a verification program and a footnote, Google’s Carbon-powered agents produced a formal proof of Signal’s protocol implementation, and AWS gave every EKS pod the option of its own hardware-isolated virtual machine at no extra charge. France named Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps as the source of the freezer attacks, and the queue behind those stories ran from Barracuda email appliances to SonicWall MFA skips. Security leads, then everything else.

item.title: The Whistle: 948 Linux root paths closed by a model, the cold chain hacked, and gVisor joins the CNCF
item.description: OpenAI shipped its cybersecurity model and the workload that proves it in the same week: GPT-6 Cyber powered the pipeline that validated and patched 948 Linux privilege-escalation flaws for about $1.2 million in API credits. On the other side of the ledger, Chainalysis disclosed that password hashes and live session tokens for all of its users were exposed to an attacker whose only public description is a phrase the company never defined. Anthropic explained why it will not fix the cross-machine Claude Dispatch hole it has known about since May, Sekoia mapped an SVR watering-hole campaign that hunts phones through already-patched devices, and the European cold-chain attacks reached France’s blood service. Zyxel’s June firmware fixed the sibling of the bug its attackers actually used, Japan announced a funded national cyber package, and Anthropic’s amended IPO filing turned “recursive self-improvement” into official risk language while Tencent’s launch post sold the same idea as a roadmap. On the cloud side, Google donated its agent runtime stack to the CNCF ahead of KubeCon, and AWS turned Hive-to-Iceberg migration into a managed job. Security leads, then everything else.

item.title: The Whistle: a Brotli patch wave, a 16-year-old UEFI hole, and Anthropic files to go public
item.description: One bug in a shared library owned the week. A buffer overflow in Google’s Brotli decoder was fixed in the library’s source in February, never released as an update, and spent the rest of the year bundled inside every runtime that links it. This October the catch-up finally ran: coordinated patches across Node.js, Python, Go and the proxy tier, and Microsoft shipped out-of-band .NET fixes on October 25. A 16-year-old UEFI vulnerability surfaced the other way, through a broken embargo. A campaign running on stolen GitHub tokens planted more than 13,500 secret-dumping workflows. Binance lost $6.3 billion to a compromised laptop in 20 minutes. Both sides of the exploit pipeline ran on models this week: Anthropic published a kernel root exploit written by Claude, Epoch AI pushed a Z.ai open-weight model through published-but-unshipped Firefox fixes at about $1,000 a target, AWS made machine-speed vulnerability remediation generally available, and Google gated its new cybersecurity model to defenders first. Security leads, then the rest.
